_meta: A sequence of request arrivals labeled by tenant, and a server capacity, used to show why a shared server should schedule requests with fair queuing -- a separate queue per tenant served round-robin -- rather than one shared FIFO queue. A single FIFO serves requests in arrival order, so a tenant's share of the service is proportional to how many requests it submitted: a tenant that floods the queue with a burst gets served first and in bulk, and the requests behind it -- from other tenants -- wait, and if capacity runs out before they are reached, they are starved entirely. This is the noisy-neighbor problem: one heavy user degrades or shuts out everyone else on the shared resource, and nothing about FIFO limits it, because FIFO's only fairness is 'first come first served,' which rewards whoever came first and most. Fair queuing decouples service from submission volume: keep one queue per tenant and serve them in round-robin (one request from each tenant per cycle, skipping empty queues), so each active tenant gets an equal share of the capacity regardless of how many requests it enqueued -- a burst from one tenant fills only its own queue and cannot crowd out the others. On this fixture tenant A submits a burst of 6 requests that all arrive before tenant B's 2 and tenant C's 1; a FIFO server with capacity 6 serves all 6 of A's and starves B and C completely, while fair queuing serves 3 of A's, both of B's, and C's one -- every tenant served. capacity is how many requests the server processes; arrivals is the FIFO-ordered list of tenant labels. These are the fixture; the per-tenant service under FIFO and under fair queuing, and who is starved, are computed.
